sources.title: Caro-Kann Exchange search snippets (Chessiverse, Wikibooks, Forward Chess, Perlen vom Bodensee)

overview: White exchanges on d5 and, after 3...cxd5, develops quietly (4.Bd3, 4.Nf3, 4.c3 or 4.Bf4) instead of fighting for a big centre. The structure is the Carlsbad structure of the QGD Exchange with colours reversed: White keeps a queenside pawn majority (a, b, c vs a, b), Black has the extra central e-pawn and the minority on the queenside, so the minority attack is Black's resource and White usually plays on the kingside with a knight outpost on e5 or the manoeuvre Nd3. Black develops the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before ...e6 and aims to trade pieces and equalise; White gets slightly better piece placement but less ambition than in the main lines. The Rubinstein line 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 stops ...Bf5. Sources call it very positional, less ambitious than the main lines, a long-time Karpov favourite and difficult for Black to win against, and say it rewards understanding over memorisation.

white_ideas.idea: Knight outpost on e5 and transfer of the knight to d3 (its ideal square), play on the kingside
Rubinstein set-up 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 to stop ...Bf5 and develop naturally with Nf3 and O-O
Prophylaxis against Black's queenside counterplay and slight lead in piece placement

black_ideas.idea: Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before ...e6
Minority attack on the queenside with ...b5-b4 (the Carlsbad structure with colours reversed gives Black the minority)
Central advances with ...f6 and ...e5; semi-open e-file for counterplay
Exchange pieces to neutralise White's slight advantage

typical_structures.structure: Carlsbad structure with colours reversed: White a,b,c,d vs Black a,b,d,e; White queenside majority, Black e-pawn in the centre
Static central formation with d4 against d5, favouring manoeuvring over tactics

character.notes: Described as a very positional approach and static; less ambitious than the main lines; long a Karpov favourite and famously hard for Black to win against. Potential for attack only if Black misplays (trap 6.Ne2 Bg4 7.O-O e6 8.Qe1 Bd6? 9.f3). Wikipedia calls the Caro-Kann more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian and says this line gives White a slightly better game.

gambit.notes: An exchange of pawns on d5; no material sacrificed (the Panov-Botvinnik 4.c4 is a separate gambit-free but sharper line).

soundness.notes: Sound for both sides; Wikipedia says White gets a slightly better game. Played by Karpov and Fischer.

structure.notes: Central tension is resolved; d4 vs d5 pawns remain, with a Carlsbad-type structure (reversed) leading to a mostly closed, manoeuvring game with a semi-open e-file for Black.

approach.notes: White's choice against the Caro-Kann, a quiet branch rather than a universal set-up. Played by Karpov and Fischer; less ambitious than the Advance and Classical but respected.

level.notes: Modern Chess says the position rewards strategic understanding over memorisation and suits improving club players. Black needs to know Carlsbad ideas and avoid specific traps; not heavily theoretical.

plan_phrases: minority attack by Black on the queenside

sublines_that_differ.name: Panov-Botvinnik Attack
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. c4
sublines_that_differ.how: White plays for an isolated queen's pawn / open game; more active than the quiet Exchange lines (not in this root's main subtree).

sublines_that_differ.name: Rubinstein 4.Bd3
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 cxd5 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4
sublines_that_differ.how: White stops ...Bf5, Carlsbad with reversed colours.

sublines_that_differ.name: 3...Qxd5
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. exd5 Qxd5
sublines_that_differ.how: Black recaptures with the queen, a different Scandinavian-like set-up (not researched deeply).

description.claim: It is a solid and straightforward response where White resolves the central tension
description.note: White exchanges on d5; the line is called very positional.

description.claim: It leads to a symmetrical pawn structure
description.note: The structure is a reversed Carlsbad: White has a,b,c,d pawns and Black has a,b,d,e, so it is asymmetrical (the d-pawns are symmetrical).

description.claim: It steers into quieter, more strategic waters, bypassing the sharp tactical complexities of other Caro-Kann lines
description.note: Less ambitious than the main lines; Panov 4.c4 is the sharper alternative.

description.claim: It is an excellent opening for players who fight for a small but persistent advantage based on space and development
description.note: Wikipedia: slightly better game for White; superior piece placement.

common_plans.claim: White: leverage a lead in development to launch a queenside minority attack with c3, Rb1, and b4-b5, aiming to create a weakness on c6
common_plans.note: White has the queenside majority (a,b,c vs a,b) and the c-pawn on c6 no longer exists; the minority attack belongs to Black (...b5-b4). White's usual plans are the e5 knight outpost, Nd3, and kingside play, per sources.

common_plans.claim: Black: develop the light-squared bishop (to f5 or g4) before committing to ...e6
common_plans.note: Standard plan; White's 4.Bd3/6.Bf4 set-up tries to prevent ...Bf5.

common_plans.claim: Black achieves easy equality and reaches a solid, balanced position
common_plans.note: Sources say White gets a slightly better game and that Black has traps to avoid; 'easy' is not supported.
